fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Reading one

fr:title.text: constvars before the semicolon, invars after

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: constvars before the semicolon, invars after

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Name every part of { lambda a:f32[8] ; b:f32[8] c:f32[8]. let d:f32[8] = mul b c; e:f32[8] = add d a in (e,) }

html:div.html:details:
Answer { lambda <constvars> ; <invars>. let <equations> in (<outvars>) }
Before the semicolon: constvars. Values closed over — captured arrays — supplied by the ClosedJaxpr's consts rather than by the caller.
Between semicolon and dot: invars. The traced arguments.
The let block: equations in dependency order (Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime).
in (...): the output tuple, always parenthesised even for a single value.
The constvar / invar split is where a performance surprise hides. Anything on the left of the semicolon was captured at trace time and is baked into this compilation, so changing it means retracing (XLA Compilation). Large constvars in a jaxpr you expected to be pure are a closure you did not mean to make.

fr:title.text: Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the shape of a single jaxpr equation?

html:div.html:details:
Answer outvars = primitive[static_params] invars
for example
e:f32[1,4] = broadcast_in_dim[broadcast_dimensions=(1,)] c d:f32[8,4] = dot_general[dimension_numbers=(([1], [0]), ([], [])) preferred_element_type=float32] a b
The square brackets hold static parameters — known at trace time and baked into the primitive — and everything after them is a traced operand or a literal. The printer shows only the interesting ones; the equation carries more (broadcast_in_dim also holds shape and sharding), reachable from eqn.params.
That bracket-versus-operand split is the most useful thing on the page. A quantity inside the brackets is a constant this compilation is specialised to; move it out and you retrace. It is the same distinction MLIR draws between attributes and operands (Position separates attributes from regions).

fr:title.text: An aval is shape and dtype, no value

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An aval is shape and dtype, no value

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read the jaxpr shorthand f32[8,128], i32[], bool[3], key<fry>[2], bf16[8]

html:div.html:details:
Answer Compact aval — abstract value — printing: dtype then shape, with empty brackets for a scalar.
key<fry>[2] is a typed PRNG key array using the threefry implementation: the new-style key dtype rather than a raw uint32[2]. Seeing the typed form tells you the key is opaque to shape-manipulating code, which is the point of it.
The aval is what tracing actually propagates: shape, dtype, and Sharding — no values. Everything a jaxpr knows, it knows from these, which is why a Python if on a traced value fails and why the shapes in a jaxpr are always fully static.
HLO's shapes are the same information in a different notation (Tuples are first-class in HLO), and MLIR adds dynamic dimensions that JAX never produces (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank).

fr:title.text: An underscore is an output nobody consumes

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An underscore is an output nobody consumes

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is _:f32[8] on the left of a jaxpr equation?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A dropvar: an output that nothing consumes.
It shows up for multi-output primitives where only some results are used — a custom_vjp's residuals when you asked only for the primal, an unused scan carry (consts, then carry, then xs), the second output of a primitive whose first is all you wanted.
It does not mean the work happens. Dead code elimination may or may not have run when you print a jaxpr, so dropvars are entirely normal in a freshly traced one, and their presence says nothing about the compiled program. XLA will drop the computation if it is genuinely unused.
What they do tell you is which primitive produced more than you asked for — useful when you are trying to work out where a residual came from (A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose).

fr:title.text: jit is the pjit primitive

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: jit is the pjit primitive

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why does almost every jaxpr from a jitted function contain a single jit[name=f jaxpr={...}] equation?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Because jax.jit is implemented as a primitive — pjit_p, printed as jit — rather than being inlined. The callee's jaxpr is nested inside as a static parameter, so each jit boundary in your code becomes another level of nesting.
That nesting is preserved all the way down. It reappears in HLO as the slash-separated op_name path, jit(f)/jit(g)/... (op_name is the trace path back to Python), which is what lets you attribute an optimized HLO instruction to a particular function in a program full of them.
It also means the boundaries are real to the compiler, not just to you: each is a place where donation, Sharding, and compilation caching are decided (XLA Compilation). Nesting jit inside jit is free at run time but is not invisible in the IR.

fr:title.text: Control flow and collectives

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Control flow and collectives

fr:title.text: consts, then carry, then xs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: consts, then carry, then xs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read scan[ft_in=((), (None, None), (None,)) length=4 reverse=False unroll=1]. How are the invars laid out?

html:div.html:details:
Answer In one fixed order: first the loop-invariant consts, then the carry, then the xs, each scanned along a leading axis of size length. The inner jaxpr's invars follow the same convention, and it returns (new_carry..., ys...).
ft_in is where the split is written down. It is a three-tuple — one group per role — so the group lengths give the counts: none here, then two carries, then one scanned input. Older JAX printed the same information as num_consts and num_carry, and you will still see that form in written material.
Counting is the only way to read a scan body. The names carry nothing; the group sizes do. Given ((), (None, None), (None,)), invars 0 and 1 are the carry and invar 2 is scanned.
The same explicit carry appears as iter_args in scf.for (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator) and as a state tuple in HLO's while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple), where the three-way split is flattened into tuple indices you have to recover by counting.

fr:title.text: The nconsts numbers locate the carry

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The nconsts numbers locate the carry

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do cond and while print in a jaxpr?

html:div.html:details:
Answer cond[branches=(...)] index a b while[cond_jaxpr={...} cond_nconsts=1 body_jaxpr={...} body_nconsts=2] ...
For cond, the first invar is the branch index and the rest are the operands passed to every branch. branches is a tuple of jaxprs, all with the same signature — which is why both sides of a JAX conditional must agree on shapes and dtypes.
For while, the invars run: cond consts, then body consts, then the carry.
The nconsts numbers are the only thing telling you where the carry starts. There is no punctuation in the operand list and the names are meaningless, so you count: skip cond_nconsts, skip body_nconsts, and everything left is the loop state. Same discipline as scan (consts, then carry, then xs).

fr:title.text: Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do psum[axes=('x',) axis_index_groups=None] and shard_map look like in a jaxpr?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Collectives are ordinary primitives parameterised by an axis name; they only mean anything inside a mapped context that binds that name. shard_map appears as
shard_map[jaxpr={...} mesh=Mesh('x': 8, axis_types=(Auto,)) in_specs=(P('x',),) out_specs=(P(),) check_vma=True]
with the per-device program nested inside (vmap leaves no primitive behind). Inside that body a collective whose result is already replicated may print as psum_invariant rather than psum — same reduction, tagged as producing an axis-invariant value.
So the jaxpr level is logical and the physical level is elsewhere. Here you see a named axis and per-device shapes; the device assignment appears only later, as HLO sharding attributes (A sharding annotation is a tiling plus a device order) and concrete all-reduce instructions (replica_groups says who reduces with whom).
That separation is why the axis name is the right thing to reason about: it is stable, whereas which devices land in which replica_groups depends on the mesh and the compiler (Sharding).

fr:title.text: Numerics and transformations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Numerics and transformations

fr:title.text: dimension_numbers is contracting then batch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: dimension_numbers is contracting then batch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read dot_general[dimension_numbers=(((1,), (0,)), ((), ())) precision=None preferred_element_type=float32]

html:div.html:details:
Answer dimension_numbers is ((lhs_contracting, rhs_contracting), (lhs_batch, rhs_batch)) — contracting pair first, batch pair second. Here lhs dim 1 contracts with rhs dim 0 and there are no batch dims: a plain matmul (Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed, A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free).
The two other parameters are where numerics live, and they are easy to skim past.
preferred_element_type is the accumulation type. bf16 inputs accumulating into f32 is the standard configuration, and it is what makes low-precision training work at all — the inputs are cheap, the running sum is not.
precision controls the backend tradeoff: TF32, bf16x3 passes, or full f32.
So a jaxpr answers "at what precision is this matmul actually done" directly, which the HLO line does not.

fr:title.text: A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does convert_element_type[new_dtype=float32 weak_type=False] mean, and what is a weak type?

html:div.html:details:
Answer An explicit cast that tracing inserted.
weak_type marks a value whose dtype came from a Python scalar — 3.0, 2 — rather than from an explicitly typed array. A weakly typed value adopts the other operand's dtype in promotion instead of forcing a widening, so x * 2.0 on a bf16 array stays bf16 rather than becoming f32.
That rule exists precisely so writing a literal in your model does not silently change its precision.
An unexpected convert_element_type in a jaxpr is therefore worth reading as a diagnosis, not as noise: it is the trace of a promotion you did not intend, usually a NumPy scalar or an f32 constant meeting a lower-precision array. It costs a full pass over the data, and it can defeat the accumulation choice you made on the neighbouring dot_general (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch).

fr:title.text: vmap leaves no primitive behind

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: vmap leaves no primitive behind

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Does vmap appear as a primitive in a jaxpr?

html:div.html:details:
Answer No. Batching is a trace-time rewrite, not a wrapper. The jaxpr you get back has no vmap equation at all — just the same primitives with a batch dimension added to their avals (An aval is shape and dtype, no value), plus extra broadcast_in_dim and transpose equations wherever the batch axis had to be moved.
So to see what vmap decided, read the shapes; there is no op to look for. Those stray transposes are the mapping decisions, and they are also where a vmapped function quietly costs more than the loop you replaced.
Contrast the ones that do appear as primitives with nested jaxprs: pjit (jit is the pjit primitive), scan (consts, then carry, then xs), cond and while (The nconsts numbers locate the carry), custom_jvp_call, and shard_map (Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name). The distinction is whether the transformation changes the program structure or only the shapes flowing through it.

fr:title.text: A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What tells you a jaxpr came from grad?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The layout: the forward equations appear first, then their transposes in reverse order, with residual values threaded between them.
Concrete tells — mul and dot_general with swapped dimension_numbers (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch), transpose equations, and custom_vjp_call_jaxpr or remat wrappers. Dropvars (An underscore is an output nobody consumes) mark residuals that this particular jaxpr does not consume.
jax.make_jaxpr(jax.grad(f))(x) gives the whole forward-plus-backward program as one jaxpr, and that is the cheapest way to see what a custom rule actually did — far cheaper than reasoning about what it should have done. It is also where you can see, directly, which intermediates the backward pass keeps alive, which is the memory question remat exists to answer.
In HLO the same structure is visible through the jvp and transpose scopes in op_name (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: MLIR

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An extensible compiler infrastructure: rather than one instruction set, a framework in which each domain defines its own dialect of operations, types, and attributes, all sharing one syntax and one pass infrastructure. That shared syntax is why an unfamiliar dialect is still readable on sight: the op grammar is fixed even when the ops are not, and Five sigils make any dialect readable is most of what reading one takes.
Collection of resources

html:ul.html:li: https://llvm.org/devmtg/2020-09/slides/MLIR_Tutorial.pdf
https://www.lei.chat/posts/mlir-linalg-dialect-and-patterns/
https://www.lei.chat/posts/mlir-vector-dialect-and-patterns/

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dialects. This is effectively a syntax. For your given DSL, you must write each of the operations in this MLIR dialect in order to inherit the benefits of the MLIR ecosystem.
fr:mainmatter.html:blockquote:
The whole structured CodeGen paradigm in MLIR prefers co-designing op semantics and transformations and let ops structurally encode and guarantee certain properties to simplify analyses and transformations.
— Lei Zhang
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The general paradigm. It seems that when you are writing a DSL backed by MLIR that you

html:ol.html:li: Write an MLIR dialect for your DSL
You can write custom compiler passes for your MLIR dialect.

html:ul.html:li: This is what is done in Triton.
Triton has two custom MLIR dialects: ttir and ttgir.
The ttir dialect is the backend agnostic IR.
The ttgir dialect is the Triton GPU IR.

html:ol.html:li: Write a lowering pass from your MLIR dialect to the MLIR dialect of an MLIR with codegen backing i.e.

html:ul.html:li: MLIR has an LLVM dialect

Alternatively, XLA ingests StableHLO, which is an MLIR dialect. In theory, this means that if your DSL is similar to that of a JAX / LinAlg dialect, then you can get a lot of the optimizations Google has come up with for free.

However, XLA works by translating StableHLO to HLO (via the internal mhlo dialect, chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal), which is then optimized by XLA. HLO is NOT an MLIR dialect and therefore in order to use XLA your backend needs to have an appropriate conversion from HLO to an executable on their backend.
This is what is done for trainium. Namely, the neuronx-cc compiler performs the translation from optimized HLO to optimized executable code on their ASIC.
Triton and the GPU backend for XLA are the LLVM + NVVM MLIR, which is the MLIR dialect for LLVM with added GPU instructions.

fr:title.text: Reading a dump

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Reading a dump

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Because the dialect is open-ended, what you can rely on is the structure: one op syntax (One shape for every op), five sigils (Five sigils make any dialect readable), regions for nesting, attributes for compile-time data, and a location on every op. That fixed part is enough to read a dialect whose documentation you have never opened.

fr:title.text: One shape for every op

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: One shape for every op

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In MLIR's generic form, what does each part of %0 = "foo.add"(%a, %b) : (i32, i32) -> i32 mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Every op, in every dialect, prints to one shape:
results = "dialect.opname"(operands) ({regions}) {attributes} : (operand types) -> result types
The quoted name is always dialect.op. The prefix is what makes an unfamiliar op findable — it names the dialect whose docs define it.
The type after the colon is a function type: operand types before the arrow, result types after. So the signature is always readable off the one line.
Only operands sit in the parens. Attributes are the brace dictionary and are compile-time constants, not Static single assignment values — that split is exactly what is known at compile time versus what flows at runtime.
Learn this shape once and any dialect is parseable; the pretty forms are sugar over it (The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works).

fr:title.text: The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why does the same op print two different ways — arith.addi %a, %b : i32 versus "arith.addi"(%a, %b) : (i32, i32) -> i32?

html:div.html:details:
Answer An op may define a custom pretty printer and parser; the generic form (One shape for every op) is the fallback that always works. Most dialects define one, so most dumps are pretty.
The consequence when reading a dump. The type after the colon in pretty form is whatever the op's printer chose to show — usually just the element or result type, not the full signature. Operands, regions, and attributes may all be elided or rearranged.
When a pretty form is ambiguous, re-dump with --mlir-print-op-generic (Print generic, print locations, disable threading) and read the unambiguous version.

fr:title.text: Five sigils make any dialect readable

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Five sigils make any dialect readable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do the five MLIR sigils %, ^, @, #, ! mark?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
% — an Static single assignment value (SSA names are printing hints).
^ — a block label (Block arguments replace phi nodes).
@ — a symbol: function, global (Symbols are looked up, values are defined).
# — an attribute or attribute alias: #map0, #stablehlo.dot<...>, #tpu.memory_space<vmem>.
! — a type or type alias: !llvm.ptr, !tt.ptr<f32>.
This is the whole trick to reading an unfamiliar dialect. MLIR is extensible in ops, types, and attributes, so you will constantly meet names you do not know — but the sigil tells you which kind of thing it is, and therefore where it may legally appear. # and ! in particular are the escape hatches every dialect uses for its own metadata (The prefix says which side of layout assignment, Mosaic is explicit memory spaces and explicit copies).

fr:title.text: A multi-result op binds one name and indexes into it

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A multi-result op binds one name and indexes into it

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In an MLIR dump, what is %2#1?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The second result — index 1 — of the op that defined the value group %2. A multi-result op binds one name and you index into it:
%2:3 = "foo.split"(%x) : (tensor<6xf32>) -> (tensor<2xf32>, tensor<2xf32>, tensor<2xf32>)
then %2#0, %2#1, %2#2. The declaration syntax %2:3 means "three results named %2", not a type annotation.
This is MLIR's alternative to HLO's tuple-plus-get-tuple-element idiom (get-tuple-element is free aliasing): multiple results are native, so no packing op is needed.

fr:title.text: SSA names are printing hints

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: SSA names are printing hints

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Are MLIR value names like %arg0, %c0_i32, %lhs semantically meaningful?

html:div.html:details:
Answer No. They are printing hints only. Internally Static single assignment values are positional and unnamed; the asm printer reconstructs a name from a name-hint interface, which is why constants come out as %c0_i32 or %cst and block arguments as %arg0.
Two things follow, and both bite when reading dumps:
%arg0 in two different functions or regions are unrelated. The name is scoped to its region and carries no identity across one.
The numbering is not stable across passes. Diffing two per-pass dumps (Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it) on value names produces noise; diff on structure instead.
The Locations are the provenance of an op is the stable thing to key on — it survives the passes that renumber values.

fr:title.text: Block arguments replace phi nodes

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Block arguments replace phi nodes

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read this line: ^bb1(%arg0: i32, %arg1: f32):

html:div.html:details:
Answer A block label with block arguments. MLIR has no phi nodes — instead each predecessor passes the merged values as branch operands:
cf.br ^bb1(%x, %y : i32, f32)
Block arguments are the Static single assignment merge mechanism. The trade is that a value's incoming edges are recorded at the branches rather than collected at the merge, which makes CFG edits local: rewriting one predecessor touches one op.
The entry block of a function-like op takes the function's parameters this same way, which is why %arg0 is the conventional name for a function argument.

fr:title.text: A region is nesting, not a flat CFG

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A region is nesting, not a flat CFG

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is a region in MLIR, and which ops have them?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A region is an ordered list of blocks nested inside an op, written in braces. It is how MLIR encodes structured control flow and nesting instead of flattening everything into one CFG.
func.func — one region, the body.
scf.for — one region (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator); scf.if — two, then and else (Both scf.if regions must yield the same types).
stablehlo.reduce — one region holding the reducer (reduce takes a computation, not an enum).
Every block in a region ends in a terminator: scf.yield, func.return, cf.br.
Regions are the structural reason MLIR can host both high-level tensor dialects and low-level CFGs in one module — a pass lowering scf.for to blocks is just replacing a region with a CFG.

fr:title.text: Position separates attributes from regions

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Position separates attributes from regions

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In an MLIR dump, how do you tell an attribute dictionary from a region?

html:div.html:details:
Answer By what is inside, and in generic form by position.
Content. An attribute dict is {name = value, name2 = value2} — every entry is key = constant. A region contains operations, and possibly block labels (Block arguments replace phi nodes).
Position. In generic form (One shape for every op) the slots are fixed:
"scf.if"(%cond) ({ ...then... }, { ...else... }) {some_attr = 1} : (i1) -> ()
Regions come in parens straight after the operands; attributes come after the regions, before the colon type.
The distinction matters because it is the compile-time / runtime line: an attribute is known to the compiler now, a region is code that runs.

fr:title.text: Symbols are looked up, values are defined

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Symbols are looked up, values are defined

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In MLIR, what is @foo versus %foo?

html:div.html:details:
Answer @foo is a symbol reference — a name resolved by lookup in a SymbolTable (a func.func, a global). %foo is an Static single assignment value defined earlier in the same region.
Nested symbols use @parent::@child.
The distinction shows up in the type list, which is the tell when reading a call:
func.call @foo(%a) : (i32) -> i32
The callee is a symbol, not an operand, so it does not appear in the operand types — only %a does. A symbol is resolved at compile time; a value flows at runtime.

fr:title.text: Every dump is wrapped in a module

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Every dump is wrapped in a module

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What wraps every MLIR dump, and what does a named one look like?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A builtin.module. Printed bare as module { ... }, or with a name and attributes:
module @jit_f attributes {mhlo.num_partitions = 1 : i32} { ... }
The outer braces are a region (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG), so the module is an ordinary op — there is nothing special about the top level.
Read the module attributes first. In a JAX or XLA dump they carry the information the body assumes: partition and replica counts, Sharding configuration, target features. A body that looks like it does too little often makes sense once you see num_partitions up here.

fr:title.text: Three attribute positions on a function

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Three attribute positions on a function

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Decode the three annotation positions in func.func @main(%arg0: tensor<8xf32> {jax.arg_info = "x"}) -> (tensor<8xf32> {jax.result_info = ""}) attributes {llvm.emit_c_interface}

html:div.html:details:
Answer Three different kinds of attribute, distinguished only by where they sit:
Argument attributes — braces after an argument's type. Per-argument metadata.
Result attributes — braces after a result's type, inside the result parens. Per-result metadata.
Op attributes — after the keyword attributes. These belong to the function op itself.
JAX uses the first two to record what tracing threw away: the original Python argument names, donation, and per-argument Sharding. When you need to know which HLO parameter (parameter(i) is positional) was which Python argument, jax.arg_info is the record.

fr:title.text: An affine map separates dimensions from symbols

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An affine map separates dimensions from symbols

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read #map = affine_map<(d0, d1)[s0] -> (d0 * s0 + d1)>

html:div.html:details:
Answer An affine map: a multi-dimensional affine function used for indexing and loop bounds.
(d0, d1) — dimension operands: loop induction variables, indices. These vary within the iteration space.
[s0] — symbol operands: quantities loop-invariant over the map's use, such as sizes and strides.
The results are affine expressions over both — addition, subtraction, multiplication by a constant, floordiv, ceildiv, mod.
The dimension/symbol split is the point. Restricting to affine expressions of dims and symbols is what makes dependence analysis decidable, which is what lets the affine dialect tile, fuse, and interchange loops automatically. You will meet these on affine.load, affine.for bounds, and linalg indexing_maps, where the map says how the iteration space lands in memory.

fr:title.text: An unrealized cast that survives is a missing pattern

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An unrealized cast that survives is a missing pattern

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast mean when you see it in an MLIR dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A placeholder bridging two type systems mid-conversion — tensor to memref (A memref names storage, a tensor is a value), a dialect type to !llvm.ptr. The dialect conversion framework inserts them so that a partial conversion still verifies while some ops are converted and others are not.
If one survives to the end of the pipeline, that is the bug. It means no pattern claimed the op on one side of the cast, so the conversion never closed. Chase the missing pattern rather than the cast.
Mid-pipeline, in a --mlir-print-ir-after-all dump (Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it), they are expected noise; at the boundary where the IR is supposed to be one dialect, they are a failure.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Locations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Value names are printing hints and instruction order changes every pass, so provenance has to be carried explicitly. The location is the only thing in the IR that survives rewriting well enough to answer "which line of Python produced this op".

fr:title.text: Locations are the provenance of an op

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Locations are the provenance of an op

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does loc("model.py":42:8) on an MLIR op tell you, and how do you get locations printed?

html:div.html:details:
Answer It is the op's Location — the provenance the compiler carries for diagnostics and for mapping generated code back to source. An op that was never given one prints loc(unknown).
Print them with --mlir-print-debuginfo, or --mlir-print-debuginfo --mlir-pretty-debuginfo for a compact form (Print generic, print locations, disable threading).
Why it is the tool that matters. Value names are unstable (SSA names are printing hints) and op ordering changes every pass, but a location survives rewrites — passes are expected to propagate it, fusing into fused and inlining into callsite (Fused means merged, callsite means inlined). So "which line of Python produced this op" is a location question, and only a location question. It is the MLIR analogue of HLO's metadata field (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:title.text: Fused means merged, callsite means inlined

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fused means merged, callsite means inlined

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do these two location forms mean? loc(fused["a.py":1:1, "b.py":2:2]) and loc(callsite("inner" at "outer"))

html:div.html:details:
Answer fused — the op came from several source ops that a pass merged: Operator fusion, canonicalization, a rewrite that collapsed a chain. A fused location may carry a tag naming the culprit, loc(fused<"fusion">[...]).
callsite — an inlining chain. Read it inner-to-outer: the callee's location first, then the site it was called from. Chains nest one level per inlining.
Both are how a Locations are the provenance of an op stays honest under transformation: rather than picking one survivor and losing the rest, the location grows to record what happened. So a long fused location is itself the evidence that this op is several of your source ops.

fr:title.text: Aliases are deduplicated printing

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Aliases are deduplicated printing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What are the #loc3 = loc(...) lines at the bottom of an MLIR dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Location aliases. The printer hoists a repeated Locations are the provenance of an op into a named definition, and ops then reference it as ... loc(#loc3).
It is the same mechanism as attribute aliases (#map0, An affine map separates dimensions from symbols) and type aliases (!my_type): purely printing deduplication, with no semantic content. Two ops sharing #loc3 have equal locations, nothing more.
Practically: when you jump to an op and find loc(#loc3), the answer is at the bottom of the file, not missing.

fr:title.text: The type system

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The type system

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The type grammar is where a dump's abstraction level is written down. Tensors mean you are above bufferization, memrefs mean storage and therefore aliasing, vectors mean register width and proximity to the hardware.

fr:title.text: Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do tensor<4x?xf32>, tensor<*xf32>, and tensor<f32> mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
4x?xf32 — ranked, with the second dimension dynamic: ? means unknown at compile time.
*xf32 — unranked; even the rank is unknown.
tensor<f32> — a rank-0 tensor, which is not the same type as a bare f32.
The rank-0 distinction is the one that catches people. A scalar tensor is still a tensor and takes tensor ops; f32 is a scalar and takes arith ops. Conversions between them are explicit.
A tensor is a value with no memory location — it cannot alias, so a pass may duplicate or reorder it freely. That freedom is exactly what a memref gives up (A memref names storage, a tensor is a value). By contrast HLO has no dynamic shapes at all: every dimension is known at compile time (An HLO line is self-contained).

fr:title.text: A memref names storage, a tensor is a value

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A memref names storage, a tensor is a value

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read memref<8x128xf32, strided<[128, 1], offset: ?>, #tpu.memory_space<vmem>>

html:div.html:details:
Answer A buffer reference: shape and element type, then two optional slots.
strided<[128, 1], offset: ?> — the layout. Strides are in elements, not bytes; the offset is dynamic. Strides of [128, 1] on an 8x128 shape is the contiguous row-major case, the MLIR spelling of HLO's {1,0} (The layout is minor-to-major).
#tpu.memory_space<vmem> — which memory this lives in (VMEM / smem / hbm on TPU; 1 and 3 for shared and global on GPU).
The difference from a tensor is aliasing. A memref names storage, so two of them may refer to the same bytes and a pass must prove otherwise before reordering. A tensor is a value and cannot alias (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank). Bufferization is the pass that trades the second for the first, and it is where most "why did a copy appear" questions live.

fr:title.text: Vectors are register-level, tensors are abstract

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Vectors are register-level, tensors are abstract

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Distinguish vector<4x8xf32>, vector<[4]xf32>, and tensor<4x8xf32>

html:div.html:details:
Answer A vector is a fixed-size, register-level SIMD value — always ranked, always static. A tensor is an abstract n-dimensional value that still needs bufferization and lowering (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank).
Brackets around a dimension, [4], mark it scalable: the length is 4 * vscale, fixed by the hardware at run time rather than compile time. That is the SVE / RVV style of vector target, where the register width is not known when you compile.
What seeing vector types tells you about the dump. You are past the tensor level and close to hardware — the shapes are now register tiles, not logical arrays. On TPU that is the 8x128 native tile you see all through a Mosaic dump (Mosaic is explicit memory spaces and explicit copies).

fr:title.text: Signedness lives in the op, not the type

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Signedness lives in the op, not the type

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why is it arith.divsi and arith.divui rather than one divide over a signed type?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Because integer types in MLIR are signless: i32 is thirty-two raw bits and nothing more. Signedness lives in the operation, not the type.
So the op suffix is the interpretation — si signed, ui unsigned — and it appears exactly on the ops where it changes the answer: divide, remainder, comparison, widening extension, shift right. Addition and multiplication need no suffix, because two's complement makes them agree.
Why design it this way. One type means one canonical form, so a pattern that matches i32 matches everything, and frontends with different signedness rules can share the dialect. Some dialects do carry si32 and ui32 for frontend fidelity, but core arith is signless plus typed ops.

fr:title.text: index is the type of sizes and offsets

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: index is the type of sizes and offsets

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the index type in MLIR and where does it show up?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A target-dependent-width integer for sizes, offsets, and loop induction variables. It lowers to i32 or i64 depending on the target, so the IR does not have to commit to a pointer width.
You will see it constantly in the shape of
%c0 = arith.constant 0 : index
feeding memref.dim, scf.for bounds (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator), tensor.extract indices, and memref.subview offsets.
Read it as a type-level statement of intent: this value addresses the iteration space, it is not data. That is why index and i32 do not implicitly convert — arith.index_cast is required, and its appearance in a dump marks the boundary where an index became a number or the reverse.

fr:title.text: A scalar inside dense is a splat

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A scalar inside dense is a splat

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read these three MLIR constants: dense<[1, 2, 3, 4]> : tensor<4xi32>, dense<0.000000e+00> : tensor<8x128xf32>, dense_resource<__elided__> : tensor<1024x1024xf32>

html:div.html:details:
Answer
Bracketed list — a full elementwise literal, one entry per element, with one level of bracket nesting per dimension: a rank-2 constant is a list of rows.
A single scalar inside dense<> — a splat: every element takes that value. This is the common case and is stored as one number, not as the expanded array.
dense_resource<__elided__> — the printer dropped the payload because it was large. The data still exists in the real module; only the text you are reading lost it.
Elision is controlled by --mlir-elide-elementsattrs-if-larger=N. Raise it when you actually need to see the weights, and leave it alone otherwise — a dump of a real model is otherwise mostly constants. HLO does the same thing, printing a big constant as {...} (iota builds indices without a constant).

fr:title.text: Structured control flow

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Structured control flow

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The scf dialect keeps a loop as one op with a region rather than as a CFG, which is what lets a pass reason about it as a loop. The carry is explicit and typed — the same design the jaxpr scan (consts, then carry, then xs) and the HLO while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple) arrive at independently.

fr:title.text: iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read this loop: %r = scf.for %i = %c0 to %c8 step %c1 iter_args(%acc = %init) -> (f32) { %n = arith.addf %acc, %x : f32; scf.yield %n : f32 }

html:div.html:details:
Answer A structured loop that carries state.
%i is a block argument of the loop body (Block arguments replace phi nodes), not a value from the enclosing scope.
iter_args(%acc = %init) declares the loop-carried values and initialises them once, before the first iteration.
scf.yield supplies the next iteration's iter_args and, on the final iteration, the loop's results %r.
So iter_args plus scf.yield is the functional spelling of a mutable accumulator. Nothing is stored; each iteration produces a new value. That is what keeps the loop in Static single assignment form and lets it be analysed and rewritten as a pure region (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG).
Both the jaxpr scan (consts, then carry, then xs) and the HLO while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple) use the same idea — the carry is explicit and typed — differing only in how the carried values are packed.

fr:title.text: Both scf.if regions must yield the same types

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Both scf.if regions must yield the same types

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How does an scf.if produce a value?

html:div.html:details:
Answer By declaring result types on the op and having both regions (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG) terminate in scf.yield with matching types:
%v = scf.if %pred -> (f32) { scf.yield %a : f32 } else { scf.yield %b : f32 }
If the op has no results, the else region may be omitted entirely and the yields are empty.
The type match is the invariant worth remembering. It is what makes the construct an expression rather than control flow — the op has one well-defined type regardless of which branch runs, so it composes like any other value-producing op (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator). A verifier error on scf.if is almost always the two branches disagreeing.

fr:title.text: Debugging a lowering

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Debugging a lowering

fr:title.text: Print generic, print locations, disable threading

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Print generic, print locations, disable threading

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Which MLIR debugging flags do you reach for when a lowering looks wrong?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
--mlir-print-ir-after-all (or --mlir-print-ir-after-change, or -before=<pass>) — IR snapshots per pass. The MLIR counterpart to --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re (Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it).
--mlir-print-op-generic — removes pretty-printer ambiguity (The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works).
--mlir-print-debuginfo — locations, so ops trace back to source (Locations are the provenance of an op).

fr:title.text: XLA Compilation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: XLA Compilation

html:ul.html:li: Dispatch / Cache: caches compilation based on input argument signatures i.e. shapes, dtypes, sharding. If shapes change will need to recompile.

Lowering: Python -> jaxpr -> StableHLO. This stage is a translation, not an optimization — no Operator fusion happens here. See chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal for the dialects involved and Three calls, three IR levels for how to print each level.

XLA: StableHLO is converted to HLO, and the optimizing passes — simplification, layout assignment, fusion, collective scheduling, memory assignment — run there. Read after_optimizations, not before_optimizations, for anything performance-related (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

What XLA ingests is StableHLO, which it converts to HLO before optimizing; HLO is XLA's internal representation, not its input format. The only thread back to the Python you wrote is the metadata carried on each instruction (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:title.text: Getting the dumps

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Getting the dumps

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Half of reading compiler output is arranging to read the right compiler output. The recurring mistake is answering a performance question from before_optimizations, which describes a program that never ran.

fr:title.text: Three calls, three IR levels

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Three calls, three IR levels

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do you print each IR level for a JAX function f?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
jaxpr — jax.make_jaxpr(f)(x).
StableHLO, pre-XLA — jax.jit(f).lower(x).as_text(), or .compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo').
Optimized HLO, post-XLA passes and matching the profile — jax.jit(f).lower(x).compile().as_text().
The three answer genuinely different questions, and reaching for the wrong one wastes an afternoon (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
The jaxpr says what tracing captured — so it answers "why is this constant baked in", "why is there a convert_element_type here" (A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype), "did my Python branch get traced at all".
The StableHLO says what JAX handed to XLA — the boundary where a JAX bug becomes an XLA bug.
The optimized HLO says what XLA built — fusions, layouts, collectives (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

fr:title.text: Only after_optimizations matches the profile

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Only after_optimizations matches the profile

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the difference between the before_optimizations and after_optimizations HLO files in an XLA dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer before_optimizations — the HLO as imported from StableHLO. Shapes carry no meaningful layouts yet (The layout is minor-to-major), nothing is fused, and there is roughly one instruction per source operation. Read it when you want to know what JAX asked for.
after_optimizations — past simplification, layout assignment, Operator fusion, collective scheduling, and memory assignment. Read it when you want to know what runs.
Only the second one corresponds to the kernels in a profile, because the fusion names in the profile are the fusion instruction names here (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary). A performance question answered from before_optimizations is answered about a program that never executed — the op you are worried about may have been fused away, folded, or duplicated (The dump filename encodes the stage).

fr:title.text: Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does XLA_FLAGS=--xla_dump_to=/tmp/dump give you, and how do you get per-pass IR?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A directory of per-module files: pre- and post-optimization HLO text (Only after_optimizations matches the profile), the buffer assignment, and on GPU the generated PTX and LLVM IR (The dump filename encodes the stage).
Add --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.* to dump the HLO before and after every pass matching the regex. That is how you find which pass introduced a copy or broke a fusion — bisect the pass list rather than staring at the endpoints. Narrow the regex once you have a suspect, since .* on a real model produces a great many files.
--xla_dump_hlo_as_html and --xla_dump_hlo_as_dot give graph views, which are far easier than text for fusion structure (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary) — a flat instruction list hides exactly the thing you are looking at.
The MLIR side has the same facility in --mlir-print-ir-after-all (Print generic, print locations, disable threading).

fr:title.text: The dump filename encodes the stage

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The dump filename encodes the stage

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Reading an XLA dump directory: what is in module_0001.jit_f.before_optimizations.txt versus the after_optimizations and sm_XX files?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The filename encodes module index, entry name, and pipeline stage. Read them in this order:
before_optimizations — one-to-one with your StableHLO. Use it to confirm JAX emitted what you meant.
after_optimizations — fused, laid out, scheduled. Map profile kernels to the fusion names here (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
Backend artifacts — PTX and LLVM IR on GPU, Mosaic or LLO on TPU. What actually ran.
Each module index is a separate compilation, so a program with several jit boundaries, or one that retraced on a new input shape, produces several sets. When a dump directory has more modules than you expected, that count is the finding — it means recompilation you did not intend (XLA Compilation).

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Related
StableHLO

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The MLIR dialect JAX lowers to and XLA ingests — the versioned, portable contract between frameworks and compilers (Lifecycle of a JAX program). Print it with jax.jit(f).lower(x).as_text() (Three calls, three IR levels).

The word doing the work in the name is stable. It is one of three HLO-family dialects and the only one with compatibility guarantees: chlo above it is sugar that gets decomposed, mhlo below it is XLA's unstable internal dialect (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal). A serialised StableHLO program is expected to keep deserialising across compiler versions, which is what makes it a sensible artifact to ship, cache, or hand to a different backend.

Read it to answer one specific question: what did JAX actually ask for? It sits at the boundary where a JAX bug becomes an XLA bug. Above it the shapes are still recognisably yours; below it, in optimized HLO, fusion and layout assignment have rewritten the program past easy comparison (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

A hand-written kernel — Pallas or Triton — appears here as an opaque custom_call whose body is serialised into an attribute (A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call), which is the first place you can see that XLA has been handed something it cannot look inside.

html:div.html:p: The same function one level down. tanh(x @ w + b), lowered with jax.jit(f).lower(x, w, b).as_text(). Compare it against the jaxpr of the same function:
Four things are worth noticing, and each is a card.

html:ul.html:li: It is ordinary MLIR: a builtin.module with attributes (Every dump is wrapped in a module), a func.func whose result carries an attribute JAX put there (Three attribute positions on a function), and pretty-printed ops (The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works).
The dot_general uses the sugar form contracting_dims = [1] x [0] rather than the #stablehlo.dot<> attribute (Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed) — same information, shorter.

The bias broadcast became two ops. dims = [1] maps the operand's single dimension to output dim 1, giving 1x4; a second broadcast_in_dim then stretches the size-1 dimension to 8 (broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims). One jaxpr equation, two StableHLO ops.
No layouts anywhere. Those are assigned later, inside XLA (The layout is minor-to-major).

fr:title.text: chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a JAX/XLA dump, what are the chlo, stablehlo, and mhlo dialects, and how do they relate?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
chlo — "client" HLO: higher-level sugar that gets decomposed. Implicitly broadcasting binary ops, erf, top-k style helpers.
stablehlo — the stable, versioned, portable IR (StableHLO). This is what JAX emits and serialises today, and the compatibility boundary between frameworks and compilers.
mhlo — "meta" HLO: XLA's internal, unstable dialect, what stablehlo is converted into before XLA's own HLO proto (HLO).
The pipeline, in full (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
Python -> jaxpr -> chlo/stablehlo -> mhlo -> HLO -> optimized HLO -> backend (LLVM/PTX, Mosaic/LLO)
Only one of the three is a contract. stablehlo has version guarantees so a serialised program keeps deserialising; chlo and mhlo are implementation details you may read but must not depend on.

fr:title.text: broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read %0 = stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim %a, dims = [1] : (tensor<3xf32>) -> tensor<2x3xf32>

html:div.html:details:
Answer dims maps each operand dimension to the output dimension it lands in. Here operand dim 0 (size 3) becomes output dim 1. Every output dimension not listed is a new broadcast dimension, and a listed dimension of size 1 may be stretched.
Two invariants make the attribute self-checking: the list length always equals the operand rank, and the values must be strictly increasing — so a broadcast can add and stretch dimensions but never permute them. A permutation needs a separate transpose (transpose dimensions read output from operand).
This is one of two dimension-list conventions and they read in opposite directions. Broadcast lists a target per operand dim; transpose lists a source per output dim. HLO's broadcast uses this same convention (broadcast dimensions read operand to output).

fr:title.text: Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do you read a dot_general's dimension numbers? #stablehlo.dot<lhs_batching_dimensions = [0], rhs_batching_dimensions = [0], lhs_contracting_dimensions = [2], rhs_contracting_dimensions = [1]>

html:div.html:details:
Answer Every dimension is one of three kinds:
Batching — matched pairwise between lhs and rhs, and kept. These are independent problems solved side by side.
Contracting — matched pairwise and summed away. This is the reduction.
Free — everything else, and it survives into the output.
The output order is fixed, not chosen: batch dimensions, then lhs free dimensions in order, then rhs free dimensions in order. So the result shape is fully determined by the attribute and you never have to guess. Newer printers use the sugar contracting_dims = [2] x [1].
The same three-way split appears at every level — as dimension_numbers in a jaxpr (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch) and as lhs_batch_dims and friends in HLO (A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free) — which is what makes a matmul traceable straight down the stack.

fr:title.text: reduce takes a computation, not an enum

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: reduce takes a computation, not an enum

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why does a stablehlo.reduce body look like a region? %r = stablehlo.reduce(%a init: %zero) applies stablehlo.add across dimensions = [1]

html:div.html:details:
Answer Because reduce takes a reducer computation — a region (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG) taking two scalars and yielding one — rather than an enum of built-in reductions. Any associative operation can therefore be expressed, including ones the dialect never enumerated.
The form above is sugar for the common case; the general form spells the region out with a stablehlo.return. dimensions lists the dims removed from the operand shape.
The init value is not decoration — it is the identity of the reducer, and it is also what a zero-sized reduction returns. Getting it wrong (0 for a max, say) produces a reduction that is right on non-empty input and silently wrong at the edge.
HLO's reduce is the same design with to_apply naming the computation (reduce removes the dims it lists).

fr:title.text: A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How does a Pallas or Triton kernel appear in a StableHLO dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer As an opaque custom call (XLA custom call):
stablehlo.custom_call @tpu_custom_call(%a, %b) {backend_config = "...", api_version = 2 : i32} : (tensor<8x128xf32>, ...) -> tensor<8x128xf32>
On GPU the target is @triton_kernel_call instead.
The kernel body is not in this IR. It is serialised inside backend_config — a Mosaic module, or Triton IR (The prefix says which side of layout assignment) — and XLA treats the whole thing as a black box with declared operands, results, and effects.
That is the trade you accept when you write a kernel by hand: you get control of the inner loop, and you give up every cross-op optimisation at the boundary, because the compiler cannot fuse across something it cannot see (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across).

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Only after_optimizations matches the profile

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the difference between the before_optimizations and after_optimizations HLO files in an XLA dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer before_optimizations — the HLO as imported from StableHLO. Shapes carry no meaningful layouts yet (The layout is minor-to-major), nothing is fused, and there is roughly one instruction per source operation. Read it when you want to know what JAX asked for.
after_optimizations — past simplification, layout assignment, Operator fusion, collective scheduling, and memory assignment. Read it when you want to know what runs.

A performance question answered from before_optimizations is answered about a program that never executed — the op you are worried about may have been fused away, folded, or duplicated (The dump filename encodes the stage).

fr:title.text: The gap between start and done is the overlap

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The gap between start and done is the overlap

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why do you see all-reduce-start / all-reduce-done pairs (and copy-start / copy-done, async-start / async-done)?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Asynchronous decomposition, so the operation can overlap with compute. start issues it and returns a handle — a tuple of buffers and context (Tuples are first-class in HLO) — and done waits and yields the result. The scheduler is then free to place independent work between them.
The distance between the pair is the measurement. In a scheduled dump (is_scheduled=true, The entry layout is the ABI) instruction order is execution order, so an adjacent start and done means the compiler found nothing to overlap and you are paying the full collective latency in serial.
That is the cheapest read on whether a sharded model is communication-bound: not the presence of AllReduce (replica_groups says who reduces with whom), which is expected, but how much compute the scheduler managed to slide underneath it.

fr:title.text: The fusion kind names the emitter

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The fusion kind names the emitter

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do the HLO fusion kinds kLoop, kInput, kOutput, and kCustom mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
kLoop — elementwise-style: one loop nest over the output shape, one element per iteration.
kInput — driven by the input iteration space. Used for reductions and transposes, where the operand shape rather than the result shape dictates the loop (reduce removes the dims it lists).
kOutput — fuses producers into an op whose output shape drives the loop, keeping a shared operand live in registers across them.
kCustom — a hand-written emitter or library-backed pattern: a cuDNN or cuBLAS convolution, a Triton emitter.
The kind names the emitter, which is what you actually want when reading a profile. A slow kLoop is a bandwidth question; a slow kInput is usually a reduction whose layout fights its access pattern; a kCustom means the answer is in a library's tuning, not in XLA.

fr:title.text: A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is a fusion instruction in HLO and where is its body?

html:div.html:details:
Answer %fusion.2 = f32[8,128]{1,0} fusion(f32[8,128]{1,0} %p0, f32[128]{0} %p1), kind=kLoop, calls=%fused_computation.2
The body is a separate computation named by calls=, printed elsewhere in the module; its parameters line up positionally with the fusion's operands (parameter(i) is positional).
The fusion op is the kernel launch boundary. Everything inside the body runs in one kernel, with intermediates staying in registers instead of round-tripping to High bandwidth memory — that is the whole point of Operator fusion.
It is therefore the unit that matters for performance work: a name in a profile is a fusion name, and the question "why is this slow" is usually "what ended up inside this body, and what did not". kind= says which emitter generated it (The fusion kind names the emitter).

fr:title.text: op_name is the trace path back to Python

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: op_name is the trace path back to Python

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do you map an HLO instruction back to Python?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The metadata field:
%dot_general.0 = f32[8,4]{1,0} dot(%param_0, %param_1), lhs_contracting_dims={1}, rhs_contracting_dims={0}, metadata={op_name="jit(f)/dot_general" stack_frame_id=2}
op_name is the JAX trace path, not just a label: nested transformation scopes — jit, jvp, transpose, vmap, remat — separated by slashes, ending in the jaxpr primitive that emitted the op.
So it says more than a source line. It says which transformation produced this instruction: an op under jvp(...) is forward-mode work, one under transpose(...) is the backward pass (A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose).
The source location is indirect. Current XLA interns it: stack_frame_id indexes a StackFrames table printed at the top of the module, which chains through FileLocations to FileNames and FunctionNames. You resolve the id there rather than reading a filename off the instruction, and the chain gives you the whole call stack, not one frame.
This is the path that survives the passes that scramble names (The numeric suffix means nothing). The MLIR equivalent is the location (Locations are the provenance of an op).

fr:title.text: The numeric suffix means nothing

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The numeric suffix means nothing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does the trailing .7 in %add.7 tell you?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Nothing semantic. It is uniquification of a name that is otherwise derived from the opcode or the metadata — the compiler needed the names distinct and appended a counter.
The numbers change between dumps and between passes, so never key notes, scripts, or diffs on them. Two dumps of the same program with one extra pass in between will renumber wholesale, and a diff on names shows an enormous change where nothing happened.
Key on metadata op_name instead (op_name is the trace path back to Python), which is derived from the JAX trace path and is stable, or on the structure of the graph. The same instability holds for MLIR value names (SSA names are printing hints).

fr:title.text: parameter(i) is positional

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: parameter(i) is positional

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is %p0 = f32[8,128]{1,0} parameter(0), and what does the number mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A formal parameter of the enclosing computation. The integer is its position in the parameter list — an index, not a renameable identifier.
Where it points depends on the computation:
In the ENTRY computation (ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output), parameter(i) is the i-th argument in entry_computation_layout (The entry layout is the ABI), and so the i-th argument you passed to the jitted function.
In a fusion computation, the parameters correspond positionally to the fusion op's operands (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary).
That positional correspondence is the thread you pull to read a fusion body. The body names nothing that ties it to the caller — you match parameter(0) to the first operand of the fusion instruction and work inward from there.

fr:title.text: ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do ENTRY and ROOT mark in an HLO module?

html:div.html:details:
Answer ENTRY flags the module's entry computation — the one actually invoked. Every other computation in the file is called by name: fusion bodies (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary), reducers (reduce removes the dims it lists), while conditions and bodies (A while loop's whole state is one tuple), branch computations.
ROOT flags the single instruction whose value is that computation's output. Every computation has exactly one, and in older dumps it is not necessarily the last line textually.
Why this is the first thing to find. An optimized HLO file is a flat pile of computations in no useful order. ENTRY tells you where the program starts, ROOT tells you where it ends, and following calls= and to_apply= from there is how you read the rest. Its parameter and result shapes must match entry_computation_layout (The entry layout is the ABI).

fr:title.text: The entry layout is the ABI

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The entry layout is the ABI

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read the module header HloModule jit_f, entry_computation_layout={(f32[8,128]{1,0}, f32[128]{0})->f32[8,128]{1,0}}, is_scheduled=true

html:div.html:details:
Answer
The module name comes from the jitted function, which is how you tell several compilations apart in a dump directory (The dump filename encodes the stage).
entry_computation_layout is the ABI: the parameter shapes and layouts (The layout is minor-to-major) and the result shape the caller must supply and expect. A buffer whose layout disagrees with this is the mismatch, and it is checked here rather than anywhere friendlier.
is_scheduled=true means this is a post-scheduling dump, so instruction order is actual execution order and not merely a topological sort of the dataflow.
That last flag changes how you read everything below it. Only in a scheduled dump does the distance between an all-reduce-start and its all-reduce-done mean anything (The gap between start and done is the overlap).

fr:title.text: The layout is minor-to-major

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The layout is minor-to-major

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does the {1,0} in f32[8,128]{1,0} mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The layout: dimension numbers listed minor-to-major. {1,0} says dimension 1 (size 128) is minor-most — the contiguous one — so this is standard row-major. {0,1} on the same shape would be column-major (XLA Compilation).
Layouts appear after XLA's layout assignment pass, so a before_optimizations dump has them but they are not yet meaningful (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
Layouts are the reason for ops that do nothing mathematically. A copy, bitcast, or transpose that leaves the values unchanged is there to satisfy a layout requirement (bitcast is free, copy is not), typically because a dot wants its contracting dimension minor-most (A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free) or a custom call pinned one (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across). Chasing copies in optimized HLO is chasing layout.

fr:title.text: An HLO line is self-contained

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An HLO line is self-contained

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Name every part of %add.7 = f32[8,128]{1,0} add(f32[8,128]{1,0} %p0, f32[8,128]{1,0} %bcast.3), metadata={op_name="jit(f)/add"}

html:div.html:details:
Answer %name = <shape> <opcode>(<typed operands>), <attributes>, metadata={...}
Two things differ from MLIR and both are deliberate. The result shape comes before the opcode, and every operand is printed with its full shape and layout (The layout is minor-to-major).
So an HLO line is self-contained. You never scroll up to learn a type — which matters, because an optimized HLO module is one enormous flat list of instructions with no nesting to orient you. The cost is verbosity, and the reason it is affordable is that HLO has no dynamic shapes: every dimension is known at compile time, so every shape can be printed (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank).
The name is meaningless (The numeric suffix means nothing); metadata is what maps the line back to Python (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:title.text: chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a JAX/XLA dump, what are the chlo, stablehlo, and mhlo dialects, and how do they relate?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
chlo — "client" HLO: higher-level sugar that gets decomposed. Implicitly broadcasting binary ops, erf, top-k style helpers.
stablehlo — the stable, versioned, portable IR (StableHLO). This is what JAX emits and serialises today, and the compatibility boundary between frameworks and compilers.
mhlo — "meta" HLO: XLA's internal, unstable dialect, what stablehlo is converted into before XLA's own HLO proto (HLO).
The pipeline, in full (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
Python -> jaxpr -> chlo/stablehlo -> mhlo -> HLO -> optimized HLO -> backend (LLVM/PTX, Mosaic/LLO)
Only one of the three is a contract. stablehlo has version guarantees so a serialised program keeps deserialising; chlo and mhlo are implementation details you may read but must not depend on.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Operator fusion
